speaker: Sean Carroll
title: Sean Carroll: General Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, Black Holes & Aliens (#428)
question: In general relativity, does an outside observer actually see an infalling object freeze forever at a black hole's event horizon?
guest: It depends on how careful we're being. If you imagine a black hole spacetime and treat you and me as test particles—so we don't have gravitational fields ourselves, we just move around in the black hole's field—that's obviously an approximation. If you stand outside and I fall in waving to you, you will see me move more and more slowly, and the light from me is redshifted. There is a limit, a last moment light will be emitted from me from your perspective forever. Now you don't literally see it, because I'm emitting photons more and more slowly from your point of view. It's not like I'm equally bright; I basically fade from view in that picture. The other approximation is that I do have a gravitational field of my own, and therefore, as I approach the black hole, the black hole doesn't just sit there and let me pass through. It kind of moves out to eat me because its net energy-mass is going to be mine plus its. I don't like to go to the dramatic extremes because that's where the approximations break down, though roughly speaking, if you see something falling into a black hole, you see its clock ticking more and more slowly.

points.core: An outside observer sees the infalling object's clock slow down toward the horizon.
points.note: Accept: external observer sees motion slowing, gravitational time dilation, or light redshifting near the event horizon. Do not credit: claiming time stops locally for the infalling person or generic mentions of relativity without external-observer slowing.

points.core: The falling object fades from view as its observed photon emission rate drops.
points.note: Accept: photons arriving more slowly, exponential dimming, or a final photon being emitted in finite time so the object disappears rather than staying bright. Do not credit: claiming the object remains visibly frozen and bright forever.

points.core: The object's own gravity causes the black hole horizon to expand outward.
points.note: Accept: dropping the test-particle approximation, gravitational backreaction, or total mass-energy increasing so the horizon moves out to engulf the object. Do not credit: vague statements that gravity is strong without mentioning self-gravity or horizon expansion.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Not really — the "frozen forever" picture is a mathematical idealization, not what an observer would actually see.

In Schwarzschild coordinates, the infalling object takes infinite coordinate time to reach the horizon, and light it emits near the horizon takes ever longer to escape. So in principle, a distant observer never sees the object cross. But what they actually see is the object rapidly dimming and reddening: the gravitational redshift grows exponentially, with a characteristic timescale of roughly the light-crossing time of the horizon (tens of microseconds for a stellar-mass black hole). Because light arrives as discrete photons, there is a last photon emitted before crossing, after which nothing more arrives. In practice the object fades to black almost instantly rather than hovering as a visible frozen image.

Meanwhile, the object itself crosses the horizon in finite proper time and notices nothing special there. The "freezing" reflects how signals reach distant observers, not anything happening to the object. Also, the infalling mass makes the horizon expand slightly to engulf it, so the black hole is seen to grow in finite time.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
No. Although a distant observer never sees an infalling object cross the event horizon, they do not actually see a frozen image lingering forever; instead, the object rapidly redshifts, dims, and vanishes from sight.

As the object nears the horizon, extreme gravitational time dilation causes outgoing light signals to take progressively longer to climb out, so in external coordinates its apparent approach stretches over infinite time. However, that same spacetime curvature stretches the light's wavelength and arrival intervals just as severely. For a distant observer, both the observed frequency and brightness decay exponentially on the black hole's characteristic light-crossing timescale—mere microseconds per solar mass. Within a tiny fraction of a second for a stellar-mass black hole, the object's glow shifts to undetectably long radio wavelengths while its luminosity plummets toward zero.

Furthermore, because the object crosses the horizon in finite proper time and real light consists of discrete photons, it emits only a finite number of outward photons beforehand; once the last one arrives, the object becomes permanently invisible.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: No, not in any practical sense. The "frozen forever" picture comes from Schwarzschild coordinate time. In those coordinates the infalling object never quite reaches the horizon. But what an outside observer actually sees is the light that reaches them, and that light gets exponentially redshifted and dimmer. Near the horizon, its intensity and frequency fall off on a timescale of roughly the light-crossing time of the black hole. For a solar-mass hole that's about 10 microseconds; for a supermassive one, hours. The object quickly reddens, fades and becomes undetectable. Light is also emitted as discrete photons, so a last photon exists, and after it nothing more arrives. So the observer sees an image that dims to black almost at once, not a frozen object that stays visible. Meanwhile the object itself crosses the horizon in a finite amount of its own proper time and notices nothing special there. The "freezing" is a feature of the coordinates and of the signal delay, not something that physically happens to the object. Real black holes also grow as matter falls in, which pushes the horizon outward to meet the infalling material.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Not in practice. In classical general relativity, light emitted by an infalling object takes longer and longer to escape as the object approaches the event horizon, so a distant observer never sees it actually cross. Its motion and clocks appear to slow asymptotically toward a halt. However, the object does not remain visibly "frozen" forever. As it nears the horizon, the light it emits is exponentially redshifted to lower energies and arrives at an exponentially decreasing rate. Within a tiny fraction of a second for a stellar-mass black hole—roughly a few light-crossing times of the Schwarzschild radius—the object dims beyond any possible detection and fades completely to black. Accounting for quantum mechanics makes the cutoff even sharper: because the object crosses the horizon in finite proper time, it emits only a finite number of photons before crossing, meaning a distant observer receives a final photon and then nothing more. So while the crossing itself is never seen, the infalling object rapidly vanishes rather than lingering visibly at the horizon forever.

In idealized classical general relativity, light emitted as an object approaches the event horizon takes increasingly long to escape, so a distant observer never sees the object actually cross. Its motion appears to slow asymptotically toward a standstill, which is where the "frozen forever" picture comes from.

However, that same extreme time dilation causes exponential gravitational redshift and dimming. The light's wavelength stretches rapidly while the arrival rate of light drops, so the object's brightness fades exponentially on a very short timescale—milliseconds for a stellar-mass black hole. Moreover, because light is quantized into discrete photons rather than being a continuous stream, the object emits only a finite number before crossing the horizon. A final, heavily redshifted photon reaches the outside observer in a finite time, after which nothing more arrives. Rather than lingering visibly frozen at the horizon, the infalling object quickly reddens, dims, and vanishes completely into blackness.
